faq.q: What is the first step in a child with fever and cough?

faq.q: How to manage a child with severe malnutrition and pneumonia?

exam: What danger signs would prompt immediate referral in a child with suspected malaria? — Inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, severe dehydration, cyanosis, altered consciousness, shock.
Which investigation is most useful when malaria RDT is negative but clinical suspicion remains high? — Repeat RDT or send slide for microscopy.
Why is artemisinin‑based combination therapy preferred over quinine in uncomplicated malaria? — Lower toxicity, better compliance, WHO recommendation.
What supportive care is essential for a child with severe dehydration? — Oral rehydration solution, monitor urine output, avoid over‑rehydration.
How would you differentiate bacterial pneumonia from viral bronchiolitis on chest X‑ray? — Consolidation vs hyperinflation.
Which antibiotic is first line for uncomplicated pneumonia in a low‑resource setting? — Amoxicillin; macrolides avoided if resistance high.
ai.title: Integrated Case Paper
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A framework for organising clinical reasoning in paediatric ward rounds. It guides students through history, examination, investigations, diagnosis, management and follow‑up, emphasising low‑resource settings.

b: It is not a disease but a teaching tool.
sections.p: An integrated case paper is a structured clinical vignette used in exams and ward rounds to assess a student’s ability to think through a paediatric problem from presentation to outcome.

b: Stable: no danger signs; Severe: any danger sign or organ failure.
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical stability and organ involvement. Use the WHO danger signs for severe disease and the WHO severity grading for malaria or pneumonia.

b: Malaria > Pneumonia > Diarrhoea > HIV/TB > Sickle cell
sections.p: Start with common local infections and conditions: malaria, pneumonia, diarrhoea, HIV, TB, sickle cell, malnutrition, and vaccine‑preventable diseases. Consider herbal remedies and environmental exposures.

t.b: Detects Plasmodium antigens; a positive result confirms malaria and guides antimalarial choice.
Shows consolidation; a lobar pattern suggests bacterial pneumonia.
Leukocytosis with left shift indicates bacterial infection; anaemia may point to malaria or sickle cell.
MUAC <12.5 cm in children 6–59 months indicates moderate‑to‑severe malnutrition.

b: Fever + cough + tachypnoea = pneumonia; fever + shivering + pallor = malaria; fever + diarrhoea + weight loss = malnutrition.
sections.p: History focuses on acute onset, fever, cough, vomiting, or diarrhoea. Examination looks for dehydration, respiratory distress, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological signs.

t.b: >50 breaths/min in children <2 years indicates tachypnoea; >40 in 2–5 years.
<90% on room air signals severe hypoxaemia.

b: If RDT negative but suspicion high, repeat test or send slide for microscopy.
sections.p: Prioritise tests that are affordable and available. Use clinical algorithms when labs are missing.

t.b: Confirms species and parasite density; guides treatment choice.
Rarely available; consider if sepsis suspected and antibiotics pending.

b: Any danger sign mandates immediate action; do not wait for test results.
sections.p: Danger signs requiring urgent referral: inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, severe dehydration, cyanosis, altered consciousness, shock.

t.b: Hypotension (<70 mmHg systolic in <5 years) indicates shock.

b: Malaria: artemisinin‑based combination therapy; avoid quinine if renal failure suspected.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Use WHO guidelines for malaria, pneumonia, diarrhoea, and malnutrition.

t.b: Use amoxicillin for uncomplicated pneumonia; avoid macrolides if local resistance high.
Administer 1–2 L over 4–6 hours for moderate dehydration.
Give therapeutic milk or ready‑to‑use therapeutic food for severe malnutrition.

b: Ensure completion of antimalarial course; check for relapse.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate in 24–48 hours. Counsel caregivers on vaccination, hand hygiene, safe water, and malaria prevention.

t.b: Confirm measles, polio, and pneumococcal coverage.

b: Bronchiolitis: wheeze, younger age; asthma: episodic wheeze, triggers.
sections.p: Differential includes viral bronchiolitis, asthma, sepsis, and dehydration from diarrhoea.

t.b: Bronchiolitis shows hyperinflation; pneumonia shows consolidation.

whenToSeekHelp: Any danger sign: inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, severe dehydration, cyanosis, altered consciousness, shock
